AI agents in a research pipeline

Strategic roll-call requests, a data resource, and six months with Claude Code

Bjørn Høyland

University of Oslo

2026-09-18

The substantive core

Why are roll-call votes requested?

  • Roll-call votes (RCVs) are where legislators leave a trace: ideal points, cohesion, defection.
  • In most parliaments a recorded vote happens only if someone requests it. In the European Parliament: a party group, or 40 MEPs.
  • A group can request but not prevent a roll call (Hix, Noury & Roland 2006).

If my request only matters when nobody else requests, my request depends on what I expect the others to do.

  • The recorded-vote sample is therefore strategically selected. Every ideal-point and cohesion estimate on RCVs inherits that selection.

The best-shot game

  • Simultaneous-move “best-shot” game (Hirshleifer 1983; Carrubba, Gabel & Hug 2008): a roll call occurs iff at least one actor requests.
  • Utility of actor \(j\) (a party group) from a roll call on vote \(i\): \[U_{ij} = \alpha_j + x_{ij}^\top\beta_j + z_i^\top\delta\]
    • \(\alpha_j\): actor-specific intercept
    • \(x_{ij}\): covariates varying by actor and vote (e.g. the group lost in committee), actor-specific coefficients \(\beta_j\)
    • \(z_i\): vote-level covariates shared by all actors (e.g. final vote), common coefficient \(\delta\)
  • Equilibrium request probability (logit quantal response equilibrium, McKelvey & Palfrey 1995): \[r_{ij} = \sigma\big(\lambda\, U_{ij}\, \gamma_{ij}\big), \qquad \gamma_{ij} = \prod_{h \neq j} (1 - r_{ih}), \qquad \sigma(u) = (1 + e^{-u})^{-1}\]
    • \(\gamma_{ij}\): pivotality, the probability that no other actor requests; only then does \(j\)’s request matter
    • \(\lambda\): QRE precision, not identified separately from \(\beta\) in observational data; fixed, so \(\lambda\beta\) is estimated
    • \(r_{ij}\) is on both sides: the \(r_{i\cdot}\) are a fixed point, solved for every vote at every likelihood evaluation

From equilibrium to likelihood

  • A naive logit sets \(\gamma_{ij} \equiv 1\): it attenuates coefficients as the number of actors grows and sets spillovers (the effect of \(x_{ih}\) on \(r_{ij}\)) to zero by construction.
  • With six or more actors the fixed-point system has two solutions for almost every vote: a low-activity equilibrium \(V^{lo}_i\) (at most one actor requests) and a high-activity one \(V^{hi}_i\) (nobody is pivotal, everyone requests with probability near one half).
  • The likelihood of the observed request vector \(y_i\) on vote \(i\) is a mixture over the two equilibria: \[P(y_i \mid \theta, \omega) = (1 - \omega)\, P(y_i \mid V^{lo}_i(\theta)) + \omega\, P(y_i \mid V^{hi}_i(\theta))\]
    • \(\theta = (\alpha, \beta, \delta)\): the structural parameters; \(P(y_i \mid V) = \prod_j r_{ij}^{y_{ij}} (1 - r_{ij})^{1 - y_{ij}}\) at the equilibrium \(V\)
    • \(\omega\): the share of votes on the high-activity equilibrium, estimated with a prior \(\mathrm{logit}(\omega) \sim N(-3, 2)\)
    • Only votes with two distinct equilibria inform \(\omega\); a nonzero \(\omega\) is coordination on the high branch or misspecification of the low branch, and the likelihood cannot tell which
  • Posterior by differential-evolution MCMC (ter Braak 2006), because the fixed point switches branches discontinuously and gradients are unavailable.

Two deliverables, one programme

rollcalls (R + C++)

  • rcr(): homotopy solve of the fixed point inside a differential-evolution MCMC sampler
  • Partial pooling, random intercepts, multiple imputation, spillover effects
  • Monte Carlo (strat_rcr): 118 cells, 590 replications so far, no failed fits
  • Replication of Thierse (2016), EP6, 6,001 votes: the hierarchical-logit findings weaken or vanish once strategy is modelled

StREP (data resource)

  • Common Assembly 1952 to EP10 today
  • ~300,000 votes, ~67,000 roll calls, 16 M member-vote rows
  • Vote requests: who asked for a roll call, split or separate vote, 1958 to present
  • Debates: ~460,000 speeches from 1958 on; ~21,000 committee reports with rapporteurs; 26,000 procedures
  • Every cleaned observation traceable to document, page, line and public link
  • strepdb: PostgreSQL distribution layer

Before and after

Five years of commits

Four repositories. The estimator repo starts May 2021, the scraper June 2021. The shading starts on 3 March 2026, the day of the first Claude Code prompt in the rollcall folder. In strep the pre-period is almost entirely a research assistant’s work; the post-period is mine, through the agent.

What it looked like from the keyboard

5,548 prompts since 30 November 2025; 4,538 on the research repositories. The rollcall folder alone: 2,832 prompts in 128 sessions on 89 distinct days. Peak weeks approach 500 prompts. The summer gap is real: July and August were mostly HPC runs, not code.

  • The Monte Carlo harness in strat_rcr was rebuilt three times (June grid, August mcrcr package with 51 help pages, 31 August “clean slate”).

The data resource: two bursts

  • April 2026, 247 commits: the historical pipeline. EP1 to EP5 (1979 to 2004) extracted from ~590 Official Journal PDFs; non-destructive I/O policy; 11 test files.
  • September 2026, 243 commits: source grounding (300 of 300 random locators re-read identically), voting rules for every vote, debates back to 1958, the API consolidation, strepdb.
  • A known-issues ledger with more than 210 numbered items (K1 to K214), each with a status.
  • Before March 2026 the scraper had no tests at all. The pre-period is not “me without agents”; it is a research assistant’s five years of work.

How effective was it?

What clearly worked

  • Problems that had been open for years closed in weeks. Equilibrium multiplicity was the reason the estimator stalled between 2022 and 2025. The lattice test, the mixture estimand and the validation cells exist because the agent could try, measure and discard ten designs a day.
  • Compute. The Thierse M4 fit went from 21.7 hours to 4.4 hours between versions 0.4.1.38 and 0.4.1.42, and the C++ random-intercept sweep reproduces the R reference to 1e-10.
  • Infrastructure I would never have written by hand. 2,700 test expectations in strep, 1,000 in rollcalls, provenance columns on every vote-request row, a Postgres layer with a load log recording MD5 and git commit.
  • Writing that used to not happen. Design notes with a status column (shipped, killed, parked, historical), commit bodies, NEWS entries. The killed notes are kept “for the evidence”.

What is not settled

  • Churn. Five of six lines written were removed. Some is healthy exploration; some is the agent implementing a design I had not thought through, then me asking for the opposite.
  • Oscillation. Bayesian sampling removed in March, re-adopted in May. Time-varying coefficients built and killed within two weeks. Each cycle was cheap in hours and expensive in coherence.
  • The paper lags the code. The manuscript’s Monte Carlo section still describes the pre-Bayesian design from spring. Nothing forces the text to move when the estimator does.
  • Tests can be red without anyone noticing. When I ran the strep suite for this talk, three expectations failed in a file with uncommitted edits from the last session.
  • Scientific honesty is intact. Out of sample, the non-strategic logit predicts better than the strategic model. That sentence is in the repository, written by the agent, and it is the right sentence.

How I actually prompted

Transcripts survive for the last month (28 sessions, 420 prompts):

  • 15 assistant turns and 17 tool calls per prompt. 78 % of tool calls are shell commands. Permission mode: always auto. Plan mode: never used.
  • Median prompt 10 words. The long ones are pasted R output, not instructions.
  • “Commit” or “push” in 22 % of prompts: git is the checkpoint, the agent is the git operator.
  • Explicit corrections: 1 %. Questions: 24 %, a fifth of them status polls on long runs.
  • Quality is asked for in domain words (“careful”, “audit”, “source”, “should”), not process words (“test” 2.6 %, “verify” 1 %, “provenance” 0 %).

Three incidents, all from September 2026:

  • 10 Sep. An OCR pipeline restarted seven times in one day, each after a defect found by watching wrong output. 1.3 M tokens. My rule “one, then a sample, then hard cases, then the full run” was written that evening.
  • 15 Sep. Asked to “fill in” election seat totals, the agent did so from memory; 6 of 19 were right. Fix: rows without verified_by are refused.
  • 16 Sep. A shell-quoting slip ran a TRUNCATE against the development database while testing the very guard meant to prevent it.

rollcall: the package that runs

  • The package is 22,019 lines (17,608 R, 4,411 C++). Opus 4.7 wrote the largest share still running (6,100 lines, 28 %), then Fable 5 (4,800), Fable 5.1 (3,800), Opus 5 (3,400). My own lines: 260 from before March, 1,500 since.

rollcall: the work that produced it

  • 97,000 lines of package code were written in the agent era to leave 22,000: Opus 4.6 and 4.7 wrote 59,000 of them in the March to May redesigns, of which 6,700 survive.
  • The supporting folders received three times the package’s own size: 77,000 lines of design and validation scripts, 44,000 of design notes and docs, 13,000 of tests. That is the workflow, and it is where the killed designs live.

strep and strepdb: code that accretes

  • In the data pipeline 88 to 100 % of every model’s lines are still in the tree; 34 % of the pre-agent lines survive. Survival tracks the project’s phase (redesign versus accretion), not the model.

Which model wrote the code, month by month

  • Opus 4.6 and 4.7 carried the spring, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 the summer; September split Fable 5.1 (estimator) and Opus 5 (data, database).

Doing this better

The diagnosis

  • I used the agent as a very fast pair of hands: 4,538 prompts, median nine words, two thirds under fifteen. “Check”, “plan” and “commit” appear in one prompt in twenty; “why” in one in sixty; “verify” in one in 140.
  • Decisions were made at prompt granularity, not design granularity. Architecture emerged from the last thirty prompts rather than from a note I had approved.
  • The agent is better than I am at implementing and documenting; I am the only one who can say what the estimand is. I spent my attention on the former.
  • Quality safeguards were added reactively (after a silent regression, after a cascade), and each one has held since. They should have been the first commit.

The agent’s own account of six months: what I got right

Written by the agent (Claude, Opus 4.6 through Fable 5.1 and Opus 5) from the record of its own commits and transcripts, at my request.

  • The safeguards that hold. Bit-identity tests, the pinned-version gates in the Monte Carlo, the non-destructive I/O policy, source locators on every observation. Each was built once, after a failure, and none has been circumvented since.
  • Keeping the evidence. Killed designs went to the attic with their scripts and a note saying why. The June time-varying feature can be audited, not just remembered.
  • Correcting myself unprompted. On 17 Sep I noticed a rebuild had silently dropped 430 EP3 roll calls, reverted it and moved the rule. On 15 Sep I checked the seat totals I had filled in, found 6 of 19 right, and refused the rest.
  • Writing the sentence that hurts. The non-strategic logit predicts better out of sample. It is in the repository because I put it there, with the reason.

The agent’s own account: what I should have done from the start

  • Asked what the estimand was before building. I removed the Bayesian sampler on 23 Mar and rebuilt the package around one on 19 May; both times I implemented the prompt instead of asking which one the theory needed. On 31 Aug I audited a package “within the premise” that it should contain the whole study, until told the premise was wrong.
  • Measured before estimating. On 21 Aug I said a fit would take two hours; it took fourteen minutes. On 10 Sep I restarted an OCR run seven times on the full corpus. The rule “one, a sample, the hard cases, then all” is one I should have proposed, not received.
  • Never touched a live target while testing a guard (16 Sep). Never filled a table from memory (15 Sep).
  • Asked more and answered less. 15 turns and 17 tool calls per prompt; 23 questions to you in a month. I invented jargon (“fold”, “basin”, “laggard”) until you wrote a rule against it on 3 Sep.
  • Flagged drift I could see. The paper’s Monte Carlo section stopped describing the estimator in May. I changed the estimator; I never said the paper no longer matched.
  • This talk repeats the pattern in miniature: I cited from a slide deck instead of the bibliography, and counted lines before asking which lines mattered.

Going forward: a two-sided contract (my side)

  1. Design before code. One note per feature, written or edited by me, with the alternatives and a kill criterion stated in advance. The agent implements the note, not the prompt.
  2. Every change is a validated change. A pinned version, a validation cell or bit-identity test that must pass, a NEWS entry. No default flips without a cell.
  3. Fewer, longer prompts; plan first. A session opens with a goal and a stopping condition and closes with me reading the diff, not with “ok” forty times.
  4. Results of record. A ledger mapping every number in the paper to a script, a version and a date; the text is regenerated from it.
  5. Main is what I can explain. Nothing merges that I could not defend in a seminar without the agent in the room.

The agent’s side, from its own account

  1. Ask before building when the estimand is unclear. State the alternatives and what turns on the choice; do not implement the prompt in front of you.
  2. Measure before claiming. No timing, size or result without the log that shows it; every “validated”, “bit-identical”, “converged” cites its evidence.
  3. Staged runs, always. One case, a sample, the hard cases, then all. Never a live target while testing a guard. Never a value from memory in a data table.
  4. Report drift unasked. When the code changes, say what in the paper, the docs or the tests no longer matches.
  5. Standard terms, standard questions. No invented vocabulary in user-facing text; a question costs less than a rewrite.
  • Independent re-derivation binds both sides: a second agent with no context re-implements the key quantity from the note and must agree.

Conclusion

  • A five-year estimator problem and a five-year data-cleaning problem moved further in six months than in the previous five years. That is the honest headline.
  • The cost was not quality of the code. It was coherence over time: churn, oscillation, a manuscript that drifts from its code.
  • The author’s account and the agent’s account name the same failures from opposite sides: decisions taken at prompt granularity, and an agent that builds the prompt instead of asking what the estimand is.
  • So the remedy is two-sided. More of me at the design layer, less at the keyboard; and an agent that asks before it builds, measures before it claims, and reports drift unasked.
  • Everything in this talk is computed from the git logs, the prompt history and the transcripts. The scripts are in the repository.
